title: The dreamer's own light
hookLine: there are no roads or chariots in a dream, and yet you ride one: who built it?
carry: the self lights even your dreams
tomorrow: deep sleep — the embrace of the beloved
last: THE ATMAN IS A PERSON'S OWN LIGHT.

cards: Last night, maybe, you were at a train station you've never seen. Someone who died years ago was there, talking normally. The house you grew up in had an extra room.
Nobody built that station, and there's no train in your bedroom. So where did it come from, and what was lighting it, with your eyes closed in a dark room?
Yajnavalkya, still talking with King Janaka, turns to the place a sleeper goes at night.

teach.h: THE THIRD PLACE: WHERE TWO WORLDS MEET.
teach.b: A person has two places, Yajnavalkya says: this world, and the other world. And there's a third, where the two meet: sleep, dreaming. Standing there, you can see both.
When a person dreams, he takes the material of this whole world, tears it down himself, builds it up himself, and dreams by his own brightness, by his own light. There, the person is his own light.

teach.h: NO CHARIOTS THERE; HE MAKES THEM.
teach.b: There are no chariots there, no horses, no roads. But he makes chariots, horses, roads. There are no joys there, no pleasures, no delights.
But he makes joys, pleasures, delights. There are no ponds, no lakes, no rivers. But he makes ponds, lakes, rivers.
For he is the maker. Notice two things.

First, the building material is borrowed: the station is made out of stations you've seen, the face out of faces you know. Second, the light. The room is dark, the eyes are shut, and still everything is lit.
People see his playground, the text says, but nobody sees him. Later Hindu schools argued over who really builds a dream, the dreamer or God.
But this is the teaching they all keep: the atman is svayamjyoti, its own light. Awake, you borrow the sun's light; dreaming, nothing lights the scene but the self.

teach.h: THE SAME SELF IN ALL THREE STATES.
teach.b: Vedanta teachers walk through the three states, waking, dream and deep sleep, to make one point: the one who wakes, the one who dreams and the one who sleeps are the same self, there in all three.

teach.h: THE SELF LIGHTS EVEN YOUR DREAMS.
teach.b: Your worst nightmare and your best day were lit by the same light.

how: Vedanta teachers use the three states of waking, dream and deep sleep, laid out in this part of the Brihadaranyaka and in the Mandukya Upanishad, to point to the self that is present in all three.

o: where the self builds a world by its own light
the waking world, seen with open eyes
deep sleep, with no dream and no desire

games.q: what's inside the dream — tap the pairs.
p: everyone sees it; nobody sees him

s: the text says dreams are made from nothing
the dreamer takes the material of this world, tears it down, and builds it up.
Vedanta teachers say the one who dreams and the one who wakes are different selves
the same self is there in waking, dream and deep sleep.
in a dream, the text says, the person is his own light
svayamjyoti: no sun, no lamp, still lit.

games.q: in your dream you're riding in a chariot down a long road. but there are no chariots or roads in a dream. where did they come from?
o: you made them, out of this world's material.
games.why: he makes chariots, horses and roads, for he is the maker. the material is borrowed from waking life; the light is his own.

practice: Close your eyes and build a place you love, slowly: a beach, a kitchen, a street, the color of the walls, the sound, the smell, all made of things you've seen.
Notice that it's lit, though your eyes are closed; then let the picture fade, and stay with the light that was showing it to you.

wordCard.voice: Dreaming. Where, Yajnavalkya says, the person is svayamjyoti, self-luminous, lit by its own light: no sun, no lamp, and still everything shows.

orig.note: Sanskrit svayaṃ (by itself) + jyotis (light): self-luminous. atrāyaṃ puruṣaḥ svayaṃjyotiḥ (4.3.9).

carryVoice: Your line: the self lights even your dreams. Tomorrow, one floor deeper, below the dreams. That's day three hundred eighty-three.
